newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: COSTELLO SATISIFED WITH ACTION OVER LEAKED DOCUMENT
Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said today that Treasury had followed the correct procedures in disciplining four officers over the circulation of a briefing paper on the South Pacific.
The report, which criticised Pacific leaders and their countries' economies, was left unattended at a Cairns conference and was subsequently published.
Four Treasury officers have been disciplined, with one stripped of his 12-month performance bonus.
Mr Costello said the law had been exercised properly, although he was not happy the situation occured.
MINISTERS WELCOME GST POLL RESPONSE
Federal Government Ministers have welcomed an opinion poll showing increased support for a goods and services tax.
The Australian newspaper's Newspoll shows support for the tax has risen from 27 per cent in 1991, to 45 per cent now.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the public knew there needed to be tax reform.
Transport Minister John Sharp said the public was more mature and better informed than it was in 1993 when the Coalition last proposed the tax.
However, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said selling tax reform would still be a very difficult challenge.
UNION ANGRY OVER MINE RETRENCHMENTS
The big American miner, ARCO, has been given until tomorrow morning to explain why it wants to retrench 426 workers at its Gordonstone mine in central Queensland.
The Miners Federation this morning sought orders in the Australian Industrial Relations Commission restraining the company from retrenching its workforce this weekend.
Miners Federation president Andrew Vickers said the sackings breached the certified agreement the company signed with its workforce.
Mr Vickers said the company this morning sought more time to prepare arguements supporting the retrenchments.
Meanwhile, Queensland Rail has gone to the State Industrial ommission today after two trains were prevented from loading coal at another ARCO mine near Blackwater.
The dispute at the Curragh mine is over a new work agreement.
CHILDREN'S COMMISSIONER BLASTS CJC IN PAEDOPHILE REPORT
Queensland's Children's Commission has criticised the Criminal Justice Commission in a report on paedophilia in the state.
The report makes ten recommendations on how to combat paedophile activities.
The report, tabled in State Parliament today, said there was a hardcore group of 300 active paedophiles in Queensland.
It said one in four girls and one in 11 boys were likely to be sexually abused by the time they reach 18.

In his report, Children's Commissioner Norm Alford expressed concern that, over the past seven years, the CJC had not been able to collect the same intelligence as his commission had during its first six months of operation.
Mr Alford also criticised the Police Service, saying there seemed to be a lack of knowledge of and interest in the intelligence databases held by other agencies.
Mr Alford pointed to the Kids Helpline database, which pinpointed child abuse hot spots such as Logan, Beaudesert, Caboolture, Maleny and Redland Bay, all in the state's south-east.
RETAILERS OPTIMISTIC ABOUT COMING YEAR
A new survey shows retailers are cautiously optimistic about their rospects over the coming year.
But the inaugural "Retail Meter" by Coopers and Lybrand also indicates that some could be disappointed again after a trying 12 months.
The survey attracted responses from 128 businesses, representing more than half of retail sales in Australia.
Almost three-quarters of them said the retail environment over the past year had been difficult or very difficult.
Expectations had improved but still more than half are pessimistic about conditions in the coming year.
However, 85 per cent of respondents believed they would out-perform the general market this financial year, with just 15 per cent expecting poor prospects.

The executive director of the Australian Centre for Retail Studies at Monash University, Alan Treadgold, has warned retailers that some are bound to be disappointed when their actual performance falls short of their expectations.
PM WILL QUASH HEROIN TRIAL, SAYS ECSTASY VICTIM'S FATHER
The father of Anna Wood, who died after taking ecstasy in 1991, said Prime Minister John Howard made it clear to him recently that there would be no heroin trial in the ACT.
Tony Wood said he spoke to Mr Howard recently at a luncheon in Sydney.
Cabinet is expected to reject the trial at its Cabinet meeting in Melbourne today, and Mr Wood said that would reflect how ordinary Australians felt.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said the discussions would be constructive, and he would place great emphasis on the opinions of Health Minister Michael Wooldridge.
"I strongly defend Michael Wooldridge's carriage of the Health portfolio," Mr Fischer said.
"I listen very carefully to what he has to say on these issues because he brings to it a great depth of experience."
ALCOHOL PRICES TO GO UP IN NSW AS TALKS FAIL
Liquor prices in New South Wales are set to rise by 12 to 15 per cent today following the breakdown of talks between state Treasurer Michael Egan and the liquor industry.

The Liquor Stores Association said efforts to secure the refund of pre-paid liquor licence fees have failed, with industry groups rejecting an offer by Mr Egan for mediation and the refund of one-fifth of the fees.
Association president Mal Higgs said the offer, made by the Treasurer at a meeting with industry representatives this morning, was simply a delaying tactic on the Government's part.
"Mr Egan offered us $26 million of our $130 million and mediation," Mr Higgs said. "His offer is $104 million short.

"The retailers of New South Wales are due for a refund of $130 million on their pre-paid licence fees and, if Mr Egan isn't going to give it to us, unfortunately the people of New South Wales are going to have pay it in increased prices." -- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
